newsitem.title: MEXICO: Maseca upbeat over new subsidy scheme.
newsitem.headline: Maseca upbeat over new subsidy scheme.

text.p: Mexico's largest corn-flour producer Maseca stands to benefit when a new subsidy system tentatively due to be launched in June is fully up and running next year, analysts and the company said on Thursday.

During a conference call with financial analysts, Maseca CFO Javier Velez said the new electronic card system was expected to be introduced in nine states in June, and that it would extend across the whole country by the end of the year.

He cautioned that the implementation of the new system was not set in stone. "We don't have any official document to say the system will start in June. We cannot have any certainty that it will happen, (but) we don't see any reason for the system not to be implemented.
Indeed, shortly after he spoke, Trade Ministry Undersecretary Israel Gutierrez Guerrero told reporters in Mexico City the card system would operate from August on.

According to Velez, the new system will provide tortilla makers with a so-called smart card with which they can buy subsidized fresh corn or corn flour, the raw material for the pancake-like staple that is consumed all over Mexico.
The card will have a volume limit, and when that is used up producers will have to buy the product at market prices.

Analysts say the beauty of the system for Maseca -- if it works -- is that it gives tortilla makers free choice to decide whether they want corn flour or fresh corn. Maseca believes they are likely to opt for more corn flour if given the choice.
Under the current system, tortilla markers are given quotas that oblige them to buy both subsidized corn and corn flour.

Velez was cautious about the impact the new system would have on sales volumes this year, because it would take time to get going. At its launch, the nine states it was expected to cover only accounted for 22 to 23 percent of total consumption.
But once fully installed, he saw rich dividends.
"It is our estimation that if free competition is in place, then Maseca can continue growing (sales volume) at around 10 percent per year," he said.

Currently, he said, the amount of corn flour used in tortillas is around 53 percent of total raw material. He expected conversion in an open market place to take that figure to 60 percent next year, and 80 percent in the following several years. At that point he expected it to slow down.
On top of that, he expected sales volume growth to match population growth around two percent per year.

Scott Weiss, analyst at D.A. Campbell in Los Angeles, said the changes should spell an eventual recovery in Maseca's share price, which was battered in March when the government announced it was not lifting the ceiling on the amount of corn flour eligible for subsidies.
He noted that Velez had been cautious about when exactly the new system would be introduced, but said if it went according to plan it would mean "positive surprises."
Will Landers of Lehman Brothers saw no reason to upgrade Maseca for its current neutral position as a result of the announcement, but he was cautiously optimistic about the long-term future.

"It's good news, but I don't think it's going to have an immediate huge effect. It's going to be slow," he said, adding he was not convinced conversion to Maseca's corn flour would run at 10 percent a year.
Seperately, Maseca announced Q1 results late Wednesday that showed a drop in profits to 125.53 million pesos from 150.74 million pesos in the same quarter last year.

Volumes had been expected to shrink because of the subsidy problem in March, and they were roughly in line with expectations. Analysts said on the operating side, Maseca showed it was taking care of its costs.
((-- Mexico City newsroom +525 728-9560))
